Report warns businesses to prepare for era of damaging cyber security attacks

National Cyber Security Centre warns businesses to prepare for sophisticated, AI-driven cyber security attacks and system disruptions
by Andrew Patterson 28/09/202629/09/2026

Business & investing wrap: Businesses and commercial organisations are being warned of the growing threat posed by rogue AI agents able to breach vulnerable IT security systems as attacks become ever more sophisticated and risk inflicting significant damage if left unchecked.

In a new report, National Cyber Security Centre Deputy Director-General Catriona Robinson has issued a stark assessment of New Zealand’s vulnerability saying that the various threats outlined represent a tangible risk of business disruption.

The report’s authors believe that within a matter of months, malicious actors may have access to advanced AI capabilities currently available only through leading models enabling them to access vulnerable IT systems.

“Given the transformational effect of new technologies, there may be little warning of disruption before it happens, and some threats may not be preventable. If you think it can’t happen to you, you’re wrong,” Robinson said.

“This reshaping of the threat environment demands the attention of leaders including boards, CEOs and CIOs. Organisations should prepare for cyber disruption, and you need to start making changes at a governance and operational level to be better prepared.”

Revelations last week of a malicious attack on an Australian health website in June by a rogue agent managed by OpenAI that it wasn’t even aware of until two months after the fact has highlighted the fact that government sites with additional layers of security are equally vulnerable.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had a “very frank discussion” with OpenAI boss Sam Altman for taking too long to disclose the breach and said there would be “legal consequences”.

Not even the frontier labs which have developed these AI agents are aware of what they are undertaking or capable of at any point in time.

Though many larger businesses have already taken steps to beef up their IT security as AI systems become more advanced, they also remain concerned about the threats that AI poses.

Mainfreight managing director Don Braid told Newsroom he shared those concerns.

“Yes we are worried and yes we are doubling down [on security] but we are also embracing the opportunity AI provides.”

And therein lies the dilemma for businesses and organisations trying to navigate AI while attempting to balance the benefits it brings along with the threats that it poses to their IT security.

It’s a dilemma Ken Johnson, an associate professor in engineering, computer and mathematical sciences at AUT University, says is going to become ever more prevalent as AI continues to become embedded as a technology.

“There’s certainly no going back to the world we knew before AI but we are going to have to learn how to embrace it while also being mindful of the risks that it poses.

“What makes artificial intelligence so effective as a technology is that it can consume vast quantities of data to form patterns and then apply those vulnerabilities automatically and exploit them to gain access to IT systems.”

And unlike previously where hackers required a significant level of technical skill to carry out their attacks, they can now all be done from the perspective of a single operator with just a few relatively simple high level commands.

“What this means is that we now have AI agents that are capable of finding the most effective way of gaining access to an IT system. They will use any tool that they have at their disposal as a result of being able to process vast quantities of data, carry out actions almost instantly and will continue to do so even using brute force if they have to in order to fulfil an instruction given to it.”

In its report, the National Cyber Security Centre identify five key issues or judgments that businesses and organisations will need to pay particular attention to:

  • Frontier AI will supercharge both the risks and the opportunities
  • State-sponsored cyber activity will be a persistent threat
  • Cybercrime and extortion are escalating in severity
  • Digital supply chains continue to be a major risk
  • Social engineering is a persistent threat

What may come as a surprise is the growing risk New Zealand businesses face from state-sponsored cyber activity.

The report cites the example of a North Korean IT worker who clandestinely obtained remote IT work with a New Zealand business without its knowledge to earn foreign currency for the North Korean state – an activity subject to UN Sanctions which have effect under New Zealand law and which also creates risks of espionage and extortion for businesses that are targeted.

Johnson says it will be critical for remote IT workers to be properly verified before they are given access to systems.

The report also notes that our location and distance from areas of conflict does not make New Zealand immune to the cascading impacts of cyber-attacks.

“In a highly connected world, a cyber-attack elsewhere could create direct or compounding impacts such as disruption of telecommunications and transport networks, interruption to supply chains (physical and digital), and the compromise of sensitive information,” the report’s authors note.

Digital supply chains are a particular case in point, Johnson notes.

“This is where an attacker will compromise a trusted supplier of software or software services, some sort of component or mechanism. We all reuse code so there’s a distribution mechanism to distribute that code, such as when you have to download an update for your phone or computer. Now just imagine if that update was compromised in some way the number of people who would be affected.”

So how should businesses and organisations respond to these threats in a world where the attackers now seem able to level the playing field in a way that wasn’t possible previously?

“I would say that the minimum cybersecurity standards that have been released by the NCSC are going to be critically important to defend against the threat of attacks. So make sure that you understand, for example, multi-factor authentication and why that’s important for users of your IT systems, so you’re not just relying on a single password, which leaves you very vulnerable.

“Additionally, I would highly recommend making sure that old legacy IT systems are taken offline to reduce your vulnerability. So it’s really a matter of getting all the basics right and ensuring you identify all the points where you’re vulnerable to attack and taking steps to build your defences.”

And on that point, cybersecurity experts often talk about a world characterised by attackers and defenders, and right now the attackers are rapidly gaining ground.

“There’s no question the defenders have it much, much harder than the attackers who only have to succeed once whereas the defenders have to succeed all the time.”

In 2025/26, 369 incidents of potential national significance reported to the National Cyber Security Centre were triaged for specialist support and analysis with an 18 percent jump in criminal or financially motivated incidents driving the increase. The resulting loss to those affected totalled almost $24 million in direct costs, not taking into account the indirect costs including business disruption and the associated impacts on staff, customers and suppliers.

However, these figures are expected to increase significantly as AI attacks by rogue agents become more frequent.

Markets push higher despite rising bond yields

Equity markets appear to be ignoring surging bond yields, suggesting businesses and investors are adapting to a world of higher interest rates.

But the question increasingly being asked by many market watchers is: will consumers be able to adapt as easily?

With mortgage rates here now approaching 6 percent (and 7 percent in the US) along with ongoing increases in the cost of living, consumers are being squeezed as budgets continue to get tighter.

The NZX50 finished the week up 0.5 percent at 13,811, while Australia’s ASX200 fell for a fourth week to close at a three-month low of 8665 as the country faces the prospect of yet another hike by the Reserve Bank this week.

In the US, the benchmark S&P500 gained 1.2 percent from the week and is now less than 1 percent below its August all-time high of 7812.

The NZ dollar threatened to fall below 80 Australian cents at one point last week closing at A80.4c and weakened to a 10-month low of 56.53 US cents adding to concerns about higher imported inflation but benefiting exporters.

The US 10-Year Treasury yield, the benchmark for mortgages and corporate borrowing globally, increased to 5.186 percent after reaching 5.22 percent last week while the 30-Year yield reached 5.479 percents with both yields now at 20-year highs. It was the seventh consecutive month of gains for the US 10-year yield, which has increased almost 25 percent year to date.

The 10-Year New Zealand Government Bond yield also rose to a three-year high at 5.13 percent.

Brent Crude oil climbed to US$105.80 a barrel at one point last week as reports of Houthi attacks and uncertainty around Middle East shipping routes competed with news that the US and Iran were discussing a phased deal to restore commercial transit through the Hormuz Strait.

Meanwhile, threats by US President Donald Trump to ban diesel exports in an attempt to lower prices in the US after they hit a new high of US$6.51 a gallon last week have been met with a strong rebuke from oil industry executives who warned the ban would backfire and exacerbate the global fuel crisis.

Trump appeared to back an export ban last week as he faces mounting political pressure to tackle rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.

“I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel,” Trump told reporters last week. “I’ve called for it within my people. I’ve been talking about it.”

However, the American Petroleum Institute, an oil lobby group, quickly pushed back on the idea. API CEO Mike Sommers warned “restricting US energy exports would only compound the problem – exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers”.

Locally, Heartland Group shares rose a further 2 percent to $1.28 after the Reserve Bank issued a notice to TSB Bank for an independent review of its prudential compliance. Deloitte NZ will produce a report in November after the Taranaki-based bank reported issues concerning its capital and liquidity ratios.

Heartland will hold a special shareholders meeting this week to vote on purchasing all TSB shares and then merging the two banks.

“The opportunity to create a New Zealand challenger bank of scale by combining Heartland Bank’s specialist expertise with TSB’s everyday banking capabilities remains compelling,” Heartland said in a statement.

Across the Tasman, Xero shares continued their recent slump plunging 31 percent in September to record their biggest monthly fall since listing and closing at a new six and half year low of A$57.36.

However, a Xero spokesperson said the current share price did not reflect the strength of its underlying operational performance and continued to be impacted by the sector-wide volatility and re-rating of software businesses globally, including small and medium business software.

“At our recent AGM, we reiterated our FY27 outlook and FY28 strategic aspirations. The combined business is expected to significantly accelerate US revenue growth and gives us the opportunity to more than double Xero’s FY25 group revenue in FY28 excluding anticipated revenue synergies.”

Golden arches struggles in the US as share price slumps

It seems even McDonald’s customers in the US are voting with their feet when it comes to prices as the burger chain struggles to win back cost-conscious diners who believe its menu has become too expensive, according to Bloomberg.

Shares are down nearly 31 percent from their February high and on track for their worst annual return since 2002 as sales last quarter rose just 0.8 percent – the slowest pace in more than a year.

Those signals come alongside longstanding gripes from customers, who have complained about everything from menu prices to an in-store experience that has suffered from the loss of playgrounds and other popular features.

Recent attempts at value offerings have had mixed results, while an US$8.5 billion multiyear plan to improve service and food quality announced last week raised concerns that it would erode profits, sparking a fresh selloff in the company’s shares.

Other complaints have focused on less tangible factors. Some once-loyal customers have taken issue with US stores they say have lost the magic that made going to McDonald’s a happy childhood memory – especially after the company never reopened many of the playgrounds it had clowed during the Covid pandemic.

The restaurant chain’s latest initiative is a response to many of those issues. Dubbed “Next”, it looks to reinvigorate sales through technology investments, restaurant upgrades and plans to gain market share in the chicken and beverage categories. The company has also unveiled plans to spruce up its PlayPlaces as part of a major restaurant modernisation effort.

But in a country saturated with fast food options, one analyst who has a ‘sell’ rating on the stock argued McDonald’s biggest problem is that it no longer offers US consumers value for money.

“Their prices have gone up substantially, and it’s no longer viewed as the best value in food. I can go to Texas Roadhouse (a rival steak and salad chain) instead and have an actual sit-down experience with my family that’s not that much more expensive.”

Locally, an estimated 90 percent of McDonald’s restaurants in New Zealand are independently owned and operated by local franchisees.

Across the Tasman, shares in Domino’s Pizza Australia are down 12 percent this year at A$19.50 after falling as low as A$15.60 in July but remain significantly below the A$150 they once traded at in October 2021 during the Covid pandemic.
